market_context: United States; aged cheeses such as Parmesan, Gouda and Cheddar
title: White crystals in cheese: what are they and why do they form?

seo.title: White crystals in cheese: what are they and why do they form?
seo.meta_description: Hard white specks in aged cheese are often normal crystals, not mold. Tyrosine crystals occur inside long-aged Parmesan and Gouda; calcium lactate can form a white deposit on Cheddar surfaces.
seo.search_intent: Identify common cheese crystals and tell them apart from unexpected mold.

excerpt: Many hard white specks in aged cheese are a normal result of ripening. X-ray studies have identified tyrosine crystals inside long-aged Parmigiano-Reggiano and Gouda, while Cheddar can develop calcium-lactate crystals on its surface.
content_html:
Small white flecks in an old cheese can look like salt or mold. When they are hard, dry and pleasantly crunchy, they are often crystals produced by the cheese’s own ripening chemistry.

Cheese can form several kinds of crystals

There is no single substance called “cheese crystal.” Research has identified multiple organic and mineral crystals that form inside cheese, in openings or on the surface depending on variety, acidity, moisture and aging.

Tyrosine is common in long-aged Parmesan and Gouda

As cheese ripens, enzymes break proteins into peptides and free amino acids. Tyrosine can become concentrated enough to crystallize. X-ray diffraction studies have confirmed tyrosine in the small crunchy interior crystals of aged Parmigiano-Reggiano and long-aged Gouda.

Those specks are part of the texture many people enjoy in a mature cheese.

Calcium lactate often appears on Cheddar surfaces

A different white haze or gritty coating can form on Cheddar. Dairy research has repeatedly identified calcium lactate crystals there. pH, soluble calcium, lactate, moisture and packaging conditions all influence whether they develop.

Crystal or mold?

Crystals are generally hard, sharply defined and granular. Mold is fungal growth and may look fuzzy, powdery, patchy or spreading.

If you are unsure, do not taste the spot to identify it. USDA says unexpected mold on soft cheese should be discarded. On a solid hard cheese such as Cheddar, a small mold spot can be removed by cutting at least 1 inch around and below it; shredded, sliced and crumbled cheeses are handled more conservatively.

Do crystals prove high quality?

Not automatically. Tyrosine crunch in long-aged Parmesan or Gouda is often prized. Calcium-lactate haze on Cheddar may be considered a visual defect by manufacturers. Either way, a crystal is a physical-chemical feature, not microbial spoilage.

A practical visual check

Hard white points embedded through an aged cheese fit the crystal explanation well. A spot that grows, develops filaments or appears in an unexpected color or on a fresh soft cheese should be treated as possible mold instead.

faq.question: Are the white crystals in Parmesan salt?
faq.answer: Often they are not. Research has confirmed tyrosine crystals in aged Parmigiano-Reggiano.

faq.question: How can I tell crystals from mold?
faq.answer: Crystals are hard and granular; mold commonly looks fuzzy, powdery or irregular and may spread.

faq.question: Can you eat cheese crystals?
faq.answer: Normal ripening crystals such as tyrosine and calcium lactate are part of the cheese and are edible.
